tests.name: Quick Check
tests.description: Timed check on Poetic Metre & Style

questions.question: Q: What is a dactylic hexameter and which types of poetry use it?
questions.correctAnswer: A line of six feet, each foot being a dactyl (- uu) or spondee (--), with a spondee or trochee in the final foot. It is the metre of epic poetry (Virgil's Aeneid, Ovid's Metamorphoses).

questions.question: Q: What is the caesura and why is it important?
questions.correctAnswer: A natural pause within a hexameter line, usually in the third foot. It divides the line into two parts and allows the poet to structure meaning within the metrical framework.

questions.question: Q: Explain elision with an example.
questions.correctAnswer: When a word ending in a vowel or -m is followed by a word beginning with a vowel or h-, the final syllable is not pronounced separately. Example: multum ille et terris becomes multill'et terris.

tests.description: Short-answer practice on Poetic Metre & Style

questions.question: Q: What is enjambement and what effect does it create?
questions.correctAnswer: When a sentence continues from one line to the next without a natural pause. It creates momentum, suspense, and a flowing effect that draws the reader forward.

questions.question: Q: How does alliteration function in Latin poetry?
questions.correctAnswer: Repetition of initial consonant sounds creates emphasis, musicality, and onomatopoeic effects. Harsh consonants imitate violence; smooth ones create calm.

questions.question: Q: What is the difference between a dactyl and a spondee?
questions.correctAnswer: A dactyl is one long syllable followed by two short syllables (dum-di-di). A spondee is two long syllables (dum-dum).

questions.question: Q: Why is hyperbaton more common in poetry than prose?
questions.correctAnswer: Poets separate adjectives from their nouns to create emphasis, beauty, and sound effects. The separation draws attention to both words.

questions.question: Q: What is onomatopoeia and give a Virgilian example.
questions.correctAnswer: Words that imitate sounds. Virgil uses 'sternitur' (he is struck down) to mimic a body hitting the ground, and 'stridor' (screeching) to imitate harsh sounds.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response Explain how Virgil uses poetic metre and stylistic features to create atmosphere in the Aeneid. Discuss at least four features. (8 marks) <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: Virgil exploits every aspect of poetic technique to create atmosphere. The dactylic hexameter itself establishes an elevated, epic tone: the regular rhythm of six feet per line gives grandeur and momentum, while the caesura in the third foot creates a natural pause that structures the sense. Virgil varies dactyls and spondees: fast action uses more dactyls (the lighter pattern creating speed), while heavier passages use more spondees (the double-long pattern creating weight). Alliteration is used extensively for atmospheric effect: in battle scenes, harsh consonant clusters imitate the clash of weapons, while in descriptions of peace, smooth sounds create calm. Onomatopoeia reinforces meaning: 'sternitur' (he is struck down) mimics a body falling, and 'stridor' imitates grinding. Enjambement creates momentum and suspense: when a sentence runs across a line break, the reader is pulled forward, mirroring the urgency of Aeneas's flight from Troy. Hyperbaton is Virgil's most characteristic device: separating adjective from noun draws attention to both and creates a complex, layered effect. Together, these features make the Aeneid a carefully orchestrated auditory experience where sound and sense work together to create atmosphere.
